description: Khagolshastra (Sanskrit for astronomy) is a team from India building a “weather forecast for the Moon”: clear sunlight and Earth-contact verdicts for south pole landing sites, using real NASA SPICE and LOLA data, tested on Chandrayaan-3. Our plan and designs are ready. We’re looking for Python/data skills, front-end (JS, D3/Three.js), UI/UX design and a presenter. Curious beginners welcome! Join us to work with real NASA data on an idea that stands out.
summary:
LunarDestination lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates at the Moon’s south pole in seconds. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to each site’s real terrain horizon, built from LRO LOLA elevation data and JPL ephemerides, so you can judge solar power and direct-to-Earth contact at a glance.

You can stand on the surface in a first-person 3D view with true-size Sun and Earth and real shadows, turn a globe lit by the real Sun, scan every day from 2026 to 2028 for good windows, and see countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset. Solar elevation is shown prominently against the terrain, and a sunlight map shows how moving a few hundred metres changes everything. Scenarios can be pinned, ranked and exported. Positions were validated against JPL Horizons to within 0.006°. A Chandrayaan-3 replay and a printable paper horizon make it useful in classrooms too.
details:
What it does and how it works

LunarDestination answers the two questions that decide whether a south pole lander survives: is the Sun above the local terrain, so the solar panels can charge, and is Earth above it, so the lander can talk to mission control? It answers them for eight candidate landing sites, for any date from November 2026 to December 2028, and for any coordinates a user types in.

The app opens on a site and its best two-week window. A first-person 3D view puts you two metres above the landing point on real terrain from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's laser altimeter. The Sun and Earth appear at their true sizes and positions, real ridges cast real shadows, and the moment terrain hides the Sun its glow disappears, because the Moon has no atmosphere and therefore no twilight. Countdowns show time to the next sunset and Earthset, turning orange when less than a day remains.

Around that view: a rotating globe in NASA's LRO colour mosaic, lit by the real Sun for the chosen time; a day-by-day ribbon covering all 26 months, with buttons that jump to the nearest better window and the best of all; a grid of every site against every month; a solar elevation panel that compares the Sun's height with the terrain in its direction and shows the sunlight reaching a vertical and a flat panel; a 2027 sunlight map around each site that shows how a move of a few hundred metres changes everything; pinned scenarios ranked side by side; and exact windows for sunlight, Earth contact and both, with CSV export.

Behind the interface, a Python pipeline pre-computes everything. Sun, Earth and Moon positions come from the JPL DE421 ephemeris and NAIF's lunar orientation model, hourly and light-time corrected. For each site it traces 720 directions out to 150 km through the LOLA 80 m elevation model and records the highest terrain angle in each, on a spherical Moon. No refraction is applied; the horizon is the terrain or, where nothing blocks the view, the edge of the lunar sphere. The Sun counts as visible while any part of its disk clears the horizon; Earth counts by its centre. The browser converts Moon-centred vectors to azimuth and elevation for the exact point, so user-entered coordinates work too. Because NASA has not published exact coordinates for its candidate regions, each is anchored on its IAU feature and the point used is the sunniest spot in 2027, refined to 400 metres. The method is stated in the app.

Benefits and intended impact

For mission planners, it compresses hours of work with ephemeris tables and elevation maps into a single screen that compares sites and dates instantly, with operational numbers such as time to sunset and exact contact windows. For science and engineering teams, it is a shared picture they can argue over together, with a shareable link for every view. For educators, Explain mode adds plain-language notes, and Print Horizon produces a cut-and-roll paper strip of the site's real skyline so a class can build the view from the Moon on a desk. For the public, standing on the surface and watching the Sun graze a crater rim makes the strangeness of the lunar pole obvious in a way a chart cannot. A replay of Chandrayaan-3 at the Shiv Shakti point, with ISRO's mission events on the timeline, connects the tool to a landing people remember: the app places local sunset there on 4 September 2023, the day Vikram was put to sleep.

Tools and technology

The web app is plain JavaScript with Vite and three.js, deployed as a static site on GitHub Pages, so it needs no server and loads in seconds. The data pipeline is Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, astropy and jplephem. Data sources are the JPL DE421 ephemeris, NAIF lunar frame kernels, the LRO LOLA LDEM_80S_80M elevation model, NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit textures for the globe, the IAU Gazetteer for feature positions, and ISRO's published Chandrayaan-3 landing position and dates. We validated our geometry against JPL Horizons: the sub-Earth and sub-solar points agree to within 0.006 degrees, about one fiftieth of the Sun's width. The Horizons output is kept in the repository.

How the project is creative

Most tools for this problem are dashboards of charts. We built ours around a single idea: stand on the Moon and look. The first-person view makes the physics self-evident, and the rest of the interface answers the planner's question, where and when, with suggestions rather than tables. We kept the detail for engineers underneath rather than removing it. The paper horizon turns a software project into something a teacher can hold, and the Moon-versus-Earth panel shows the same 24 hours on both worlds on one chart.

Factors we considered

Scientific correctness first: no atmosphere means no refraction and a horizon defined by terrain and the curve of the Moon, and we checked that the computed horizon reproduces the theoretical edge of the sphere exactly. Honesty about limits: terrain covers 80 to 90 degrees south, so sites outside it use a smooth-sphere horizon and are labelled; Earth visibility is line of sight, not a link budget; panel figures are sunlight, not electrical output; the ground texture is generated detail while the shape and shadows are real data. Three audiences on one screen without mode switching. Speed, by pre-computing everything so the page responds instantly. And NASA's own guidance for this challenge: rapid comparison, clear time-to-sunset, solar elevation shown prominently, the contrast with Earth, and the sensitivity to small changes in place and date.
